🐾 Here’s the story behind Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase**.

From **August 2009 to June 2012**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for payments capabilities within ACCESS Next Generation, the bank’s global corporate banking portal. The bank’s regional systems had different payment formats, client configurations, entitlement structures, and compliance requirements. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but its out-of-box capabilities did not cover the requirements of **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth, New Hampshire offices, determining where native platform capabilities ended and custom engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH credits and direct debits, wires, FX/cross-border payments, and federal tax payments. That included NACHA file validation, foreign exchange engine integration, and Message Authentication Code security so corporate users could validate payment integrity before release. He also delivered the centralized payments gateway, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**.

The work extended into access controls, compliance, and production operations. Matt built payment-type-specific permissions, such as authorizing wire approval without allowing FX initiation. Bulk permission changes and role-based profiles reduced entitlement management from **days to minutes**. He mapped regional regulatory requirements into data visibility and access controls, sequenced launches by regulatory readiness, and owned on-call and critical production incident response.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. The payments gateway gave corporate treasurers a single entry point across regions, replacing fragmented integrations and separate local logins. Legacy client configurations, entitlements, and transaction histories were migrated **without disruption to live payment operations**, and the regional compliance framework enabled rollout across APAC, EMEA, and the Americas **without regulatory blockers**.

🐾 Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose.

Teams he inherited were often “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His philosophy starts with trust, clarity, and shared purpose, rather than more process or tools. He makes intent explicit, pushes decisions to the people closest to the work, and coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, he put engineers, product managers, and UX architects into balanced teams with equal participation and shared accountability. Instead of handing work between separate functions, they used pair programming, collaborative coding, stand-ups, and retrospectives. He connected team goals to client and business outcomes, embedded clients into the teams, and used user research and iteration reviews to decide what to build next.

His “permit to fail” environment addressed teams’ fear of blame. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasized lessons rather than finger-pointing, and supported low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses. In product incubation, he set expectations upfront that prototypes and user tests would likely fail. Teams used those results to challenge assumptions and shape product direction week by week, before committing to costly builds.

He paired that freedom with automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices, including TDD and continuous integration. At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also produced **zero-defect production code**, reduced handoffs, and fewer project delays.

question: Why hire Matt?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt’s assumptions led to a real client incident.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying the configuration, he assumed the IAM controls and environment boundaries were correct. He relied on inherited documentation, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify that production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Following the incident, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His own wording for the lesson was: “assumptions are risks in disguise.”

🐾 Here’s a time Matt’s assumptions led to a real client incident.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500 financial services client**. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production environments. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying the configuration, he assumed the IAM controls and environment boundaries were correct. He relied on inherited documentation, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not verify that production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. He also had not implemented compensating controls such as data masking or email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.” Following the incident, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His own wording for the lesson was: “assumptions are risks in disguise.”

🐾 Here’s how Matt built AWS Launchpad.

At **Accenture’s** Liquid Studio, traditional training programs couldn’t keep pace with rapidly evolving AWS technologies. Engineers had gaps in cloud competency, and cloud adoption was slowing. The Atlanta Innovation Hub needed a structured program that would help engineers earn certifications and apply cloud skills to cloud-native initiatives.

From July **2018** to November **2019**, Matt led AWS Launchpad in collaboration with AWS. He designed structured learning paths and certification programs covering core services, including Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB, Kubernetes, and ECS/Fargate, alongside cloud-native application development.

Instead of relying on theory alone, Matt delivered interactive workshops and hands-on labs that immersed engineers in real-world AWS environments. Practical application was part of the training, not something participants had to figure out after completing it.

He also established cloud expert mentorship teams so engineers had people to learn from as they developed their skills. Group coaching sessions and knowledge-sharing workshops gave participants additional opportunities to work through questions and share what they were learning. The program combined structured learning, practical exercises, and ongoing support rather than treating certification as a standalone exam-preparation activity.

More than **200 professionals earned AWS certifications**, including AWS Solutions Architect and DevOps Engineer certifications. Engineers gained cloud competencies to lead cloud transformation projects, and the program accelerated cloud adoption and the launch of cloud-native initiatives at **Accenture**.
